extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and literary critics of English drama/poetry (readers interested in standards for dramatic and poetic quality)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for judging and producing English plays and poems, with attention to language, wit, plotting, character, and suitability to contemporary conversation and audience. Emphasises refinement (improvement) of wit, language, and conversation as marks of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of the age (overall standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our Wit, Language and Conversation; or, an alteration in them for the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this triple test (wit, language, conversation) as the organising standard when claiming that current writing is superior to past ages. The essay treats progress in drama and poetry as legitimate when these three elements are demonstrably improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language refinement — reject improper older forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement consists in rejecting such old words or phrases which are ill sounding or improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between words antiquated by custom (accidental loss) and words that are improper; only the latter count as real improvements when removed. Examples of faults to avoid: solecisms, misplaced prepositions, wrong articles, redundant pronouns, incorrect number (e.g., 'ones' plural), and antiquated or incorrect syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language refinement — admit useful new words
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement consists in admitting new words which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted words must enrich the tongue (like bullion). Some adoptions are ornamental, making language more courtly; poets who borrow new words should do so sparingly and wait until custom familiarizes them. Examples: some French imports became naturalized (good graces, minuet, chagrin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of grammar and sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid solecisms of speech and notorious flaws in sense; pages should be correct in both language and sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by many quoted lines from Jonson and Shakespeare where prepositions placed at line end, false pronoun agreement, incorrect articles, or redundant words create errors. Being the first to observe such errors is important to correcting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-placing of words for sweetness (prosody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry uses well-placing of words for the sweetness of pronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prosodic concern (placement for sound) is praised as introduced by Mr Waller. Avoid constructions that ruin cadence or force awkward placements solely for rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affected foreign idiom (sophistication vs. corruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not corrupt English idiom by mixing it too much with French; sophistication of language is not necessarily improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writers who 'turn English into French' by overusing French phrases for fashion. Borrowings should be measured and only valuable snippets preserved ('aurum ex stercore colligere').

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic innovation by semantic grafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets improve language by applying received words to a new signification (grafting new sense onto old words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace's precept cited: 'Reddiderit junctura novum'—using tropes and metaphors to heighten signification is praised (Horace, Odes). This is a legitimate route to refinement and beauty of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot quality and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots should be correctly constructed, coherent, and avoid lameness or impossible foundations; the decorum of the stage must be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes many old plots as 'ridiculous incoherent story' spanning whole plays (Pericles, Winter's Tale, Measure for Measure). Good plotting involves proper development and avoiding improbable incidents that undermine audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum and appropriateness of diction by genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction must match the genre: e.g., tragedy ought to be higher and more sonorous than other kinds of poetry; meanness of expression is inappropriate in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lines from Catiline show meanness inappropriate to tragedy. Maintain grandeur of style where the genre requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and maintenance of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be consistently portrayed and their chosen traits maintained to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jonson is praised for choice and maintenance of characters; Fletcher and Shakespeare are criticised where characters slip (e.g., Philaster's violent acts and immediate comic diversion by a clown). Ensure scenes serve character continuity and dramatic effect without breaking tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and avoidance of redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid redundant words and constructions (e.g., unnecessary pronouns, repeated prepositions, double comparatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'they' redundant; 'more stricter' as gross two comparatives. Redundancy harms clarity and elegance; editors should remove unnecessary particles and tighten expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and steadiness of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit should be appropriate to the dignity of the subject and steady — avoid plunging from high thought into low expressions or slumping mid-play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's genius is praised but faulted for precipitous drops from great thought to low expressions; Fletcher's luxuriance often causes him to 'not know when to give over' leading to slump in later acts. Aim for steadiness: if early scenes are strong, sustain that quality throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of lowest groveling wit (clenches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the lowest, most groveling kind of wit (clenches) which degrade discourse, even when spoken by witty characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Jonson and earlier writers often use 'clenches' and mean coarse jokes; such devices may be historically common but are undesirable if they lower the overall tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtliness and refinement of manners (conversation reflected in writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy and characters should reflect the courtly gallantry and civility of contemporary conversation; refined conversation improves dramatic writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay attributes modern improvements to court example (Charles II) and continental travel. Gentlemen characters should display urbane raillery rather than clownishness or tankard-folly; audiences prefer the follies of their own social circle rather than ragged clownery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience suitability and address
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with regard to the actual audience and their tastes; the stage's nature and audience composition shape the play's demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare wrote to rough, popular theatres and tailored effects to that audience; Dryden addressed a courtly, critical audience. Honesty about whom you address explains certain irregularities and should inform compositional choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of severe criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A severe critic acts as a friend by keeping poets within bounds; critical strictness aids improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that severe critics prevent poets' luxuriancy from overleaping good bounds; critical feedback is constructive and necessary for refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment in ordering plot and choice of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Good dramatic art requires judgment in ordering of plot, choice of characters, and maintaining chosen elements to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jonson is commended for these qualities; they are presented as technical virtues of dramatic composition that younger writers should emulate.
